entities.name: Dawlat Berdi
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Dawlat Berdi, also known as Devlet Berdi, emerged as a pivotal, albeit transient, figure in the tumultuous political landscape of the Golden Horde during the early 15th century. Reigning intermittently as Khan from 1419 to 1421 and again from 1428 until his death in 1432, he represented a desperate attempt to restore stability to a fragmenting empire that once dominated vast swathes of Eastern Europe and Central Asia. A direct descendant of Berke Khan, the grandson of Genghis Khan and an early convert to Islam, Dawlat Berdi's rule was characterized by relentless internal strife among rival Chinggisid claimants and external pressures from rising regional powers. His brief periods of authority underscore the profound crisis of succession and decentralization that ultimately led to the dissolution of the unified Golden Horde.

Dawlat Berdi's ascent to power was marked by a brutal power struggle following the assassination of his cousin, Ulugh Muhammad, in 1419. He initially seized control of Sarai, the Golden Horde's traditional capital, but his authority was immediately challenged by other contenders, including Borak Khan and Hacı I Giray, founder of the Crimean Khanate. His second reign, commencing in 1428, saw him consolidate some influence over the Crimean peninsula and parts of the Volga region, minting coins in his name, a traditional sign of sovereign authority. However, his efforts to re-establish a stable central government were severely undermined by constant warfare against rival khans, particularly Ulugh Muhammad, who eventually re-emerged as a dominant force.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Dawlat Berdi's tumultuous and intermittent reign as Khan of the Golden Horde from 1419 to 1432 significantly contributed to the irreversible fragmentation of the once-mighty Mongol successor state. His persistent struggles against rivals like Ulugh Muhammad accelerated the decline of central authority, directly paving the way for the emergence of independent regional khanates such as the Crimean and Kazan.
